name: North Carolina

notes: Food is exempt from the state tax and taxed at a 2% local rate (transit and other local taxes don't apply to it), but candy, soft drinks and dietary supplements are taxed at the full rate, which is not counted here.

Alcohol bought in stores: beer, wine and drinks served are taxed at the full rate. Liquor from ABC stores is taxed at a flat 7% everywhere (no transit tax or Mecklenburg's 1%), on top of a 30% excise in its price; it isn't separated here, since no official figure gives liquor's share of alcohol bought in stores, so the full local rate is used. (Liquor stores' national share of alcohol bought in stores, used for Mississippi's taxes on package stores, doesn't fit: it counts beer and wine shops too, and this rate falls on liquor, not on a kind of store.).
Cigarettes and other tobacco are taxed at the general rate, on top of their excise taxes.
Barber and beauty services: not taxed (FTA 2017 survey answer).
Laundry and dry cleaning are taxed, except coin-, token- or card-operated washers and dryers, which is not taken out here.
Motor fuel is exempt from sales tax. The per-gallon excise tax (41 cents in 2026), left out here, is suspended October 10 through November 30, 2026.
Auto repair labor: taxed (FTA 2017 survey answer).
Diapers and menstrual products are taxed (only diapers sold on prescription are exempt; a 2026 House bill to exempt them, H1200, did not become law). Clothing has had no sales tax holiday since 2014.
gaps: North Carolina has no city sales taxes; each county's rate (2% or 2.25% local) plus the 0.5% transit taxes (Durham, Mecklenburg, Orange and Wake) and the 1% Mecklenburg tax that started July 1, 2026 apply to the whole county.
Food for home consumption is taxed at 2% local only, which the grocery category uses; it isn't part of the general rate here.
Some address records in Dare County still point to a special district (code 99055) with no current rate, last listed at 1% from January 1, 2006 to June 30, 2006; it is counted as 0.

Local 1% taxes on prepared food and drink are counted in the restaurant rate for Mecklenburg, Wake, Cumberland and Dare counties and the town of Hillsborough, the five places that levy one; Durham has none (its voters turned one down in 2008). Local hotel occupancy taxes are not counted.

tiers.label: North Carolina county development tier
tiers.what: Tier 1 (most distressed) to Tier 3 (least distressed) under G.S. §143B-437.08; the tier sets eligibility, local match requirements and award levels for various state economic development programs and grants.

programs: Municipal service districts (business improvement districts) are mapped for Charlotte, Raleigh, Durham, Winston-Salem, Fayetteville, Salisbury, Goldsboro, Asheville, Greensboro (its downtown Business Improvement District and the College Hill and Dunleath districts) and Wilmington. No map was found for Chapel Hill's. Greenville levies no municipal service district: the Department of Revenue's report of local property taxes for 2024-25 shows no municipal special district levy in Pitt County (the Uptown district on the city's layer isn't one). High Point put its proposed district on hold in February 2026, as reported. Greensboro's seven active redevelopment areas are mapped; other cities' aren't.

Local governments in Tier 1 and Tier 2 counties, and in census tracts with fewer than 500 people per square mile in Tier 3 counties, can get the Department of Commerce's rural building reuse and infrastructure grants; the tier is shown for each county, but the low-density Tier 3 tracts aren't marked. Main Street communities aren't shown: the Department's map of them dates from 2018, and it publishes no current list. North Carolina's project development financing districts (its form of TIF) are rare, and no official map or current list was found (the Local Government Commission approves their bonds; a 2008 UNC School of Government bulletin counted three).

warn.text: Asheville draws many visitors, but the area shown here isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (under 2%) and its lodging places per resident fall under the flag's cutoffs, though 7 of its 23 census tracts are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of Asheville's local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

warn: Hurricane Helene's flood in September 2024 destroyed about 45 buildings in Chimney Rock, nearly a third of the village's businesses (Post and Courier, September 2025); the village reopened to visitors in July 2025. This page's figures come from before the storm.

After Hurricane Helene in September 2024, the lake at Lake Lure was closed to boating and swimming while crews spent more than a year removing debris; it reopened to visitors for Memorial Day weekend 2026 (ABC11, May 22, 2026). This page's store and job figures come from before the storm.
